subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 grammar task on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: In the sentence "The frightened child ran quickly", which word is an adjective?
options: ran
quickly
frightened
child
questions.explain: An adjective describes a noun. 'Frightened' describes the noun 'child'. 'Quickly' is an adverb (it describes the verb 'ran').

questions.q: In "She hid the letter under the floorboards", what word class is 'under'?
options: Adverb
Preposition
Conjunction
Determiner
questions.explain: 'Under' shows the position of the letter in relation to the floorboards, so it is a preposition.

questions.q: Which word class joins two clauses together, such as 'and', 'but' or 'because'?
options: Pronoun
Determiner
Conjunction
Adverb
questions.explain: A conjunction joins words, phrases or clauses. 'And', 'but' and 'because' are all conjunctions.

questions.q: "I finished my dinner and then I washed up." What type of sentence is this?
options: Simple
Compound
Complex
Not a full sentence
questions.explain: Two main clauses ('I finished my dinner' / 'I washed up') are joined by the coordinating conjunction 'and'. Two main clauses joined this way make a compound sentence.

questions.q: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
options: The dog barked at the postman.
The dog barked and the cat hissed.
Because the postman was late, the dog barked.
The dog. The postman.
questions.explain: A complex sentence has a main clause plus a subordinate clause. 'Because the postman was late' is a subordinate clause (it cannot stand alone) attached to the main clause 'the dog barked'.

questions.q: What is a clause?
options: Any group of two or more words
A group of words containing its own verb
A word that describes a noun
A punctuation mark
questions.explain: A clause is a group of words built around its own verb. A main clause makes sense on its own; a subordinate clause does not.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
options: The dog wagged it's tail.
The dog wagged its tail.
The dog wagged its' tail.
The dog wagged it,s tail.
questions.explain: 'Its' (no apostrophe) shows belonging. 'It's' only ever means 'it is' or 'it has'. Here the tail belongs to the dog, so 'its' is correct.

questions.q: How should you write the possessive for a lead belonging to more than one dog?
options: the dogs lead
the dog's lead
the dogs' lead
the dogs's lead
questions.explain: For a plural noun that already ends in 's', add the apostrophe after the s: 'the dogs' lead' means the lead belonging to several dogs.

questions.q: Which sentence contains a comma splice (a common error)?
options: It was late, so we went home.
It was late, we went home.
Because it was late, we went home.
It was late; we went home.
questions.explain: A comma splice joins two complete sentences with only a comma. 'It was late, we went home' does this. Fix it with 'so', a full stop, or a semicolon.

questions.q: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
options: She needed: a pen, a ruler and a rubber.
She needed three things: a pen, a ruler and a rubber.
She needed three things; a pen a ruler and a rubber.
She: needed three things a pen, a ruler and a rubber.
questions.explain: A colon introduces a list or explanation, and the part before it must be a complete clause. 'She needed three things' is a full clause, so the colon is correct.

questions.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
options: The rain stopped; and the sun came out.
The rain stopped; the sun came out.
The rain stopped; because the sun came out.
The rain; stopped the sun came out.
questions.explain: A semicolon links two closely related complete sentences. 'The rain stopped' and 'the sun came out' are both full sentences, so the semicolon joins them correctly (and you don't add 'and' as well).

questions.q: Which line of speech is punctuated correctly?
options: "Where are you going" she asked.
"Where are you going?" she asked.
"Where are you going?", she asked.
Where are you going? "she asked".
questions.explain: The question mark goes inside the closing speech marks, and no extra comma is needed after them. '"Where are you going?" she asked.' is correct.

questions.q: Which sentence is written in correct Standard English?
options: We was really tired after the match.
We were really tired after the match.
We is really tired after the match.
We been really tired after the match.
questions.explain: The plural subject 'we' needs the plural verb form 'were'. 'We was' is non-standard; in Standard English it is 'we were'.

questions.q: Which sentence uses there, their and they're correctly?
options: Their going to leave they're coats over there.
They're going to leave their coats over there.
There going to leave their coats over they're.
They're going to leave there coats over their.
questions.explain: 'They're' = they are; 'their' = belonging to them; 'there' = a place. Only the second sentence uses all three correctly.

questions.q: Which sentence keeps the tense consistent?
options: He opened the door and walks inside.
He opens the door and walked inside.
He opened the door and walked inside.
He open the door and walk inside.
questions.explain: Both verbs should stay in the past tense: 'opened' and 'walked'. Mixing past and present ('opened... walks') is a common tense error.

questions.q: Choose the sentence with correct subject-verb agreement.
options: The box of chocolates are on the table.
The box of chocolates is on the table.
The box of chocolates were on the table.
The box of chocolates be on the table.
questions.explain: The subject is 'the box' (singular), not 'chocolates', so it needs the singular verb 'is'. Don't be tricked by the plural noun nearest the verb.

questions.q: The word 'misunderstand' contains the prefix 'mis-'. What does this prefix mean?
options: again
before
wrongly
very
questions.explain: The prefix 'mis-' means 'wrongly' or 'badly', so 'misunderstand' means to understand wrongly.

questions.q: Adding the suffix '-less' to 'hope' creates 'hopeless'. What does the suffix '-less' mean?
options: full of
without
the state of
able to
questions.explain: The suffix '-less' means 'without', so 'hopeless' means without hope. Compare '-ful' (full of), as in 'hopeful'.

questions.q: A writer follows several long sentences with the short sentence: "Then silence." What is the most likely effect?
options: It makes the writing more formal.
It creates a sudden, dramatic pause for tension.
It shows the writer made a mistake.
It changes the tense of the passage.
questions.explain: Dropping to a very short sentence after long ones jolts the reader and creates tension or drama. Varying sentence length is a deliberate choice for effect.

questions.q: Which change makes this sentence more vivid: 'The man went into the room'?
options: The man went into the room quickly.
The man, who was tall, went into the room.
The stranger crept into the room.
The man went into the big room.
questions.explain: Choosing a precise noun ('stranger') and a precise verb ('crept') paints a clearer, more atmospheric picture than simply adding extra words to vague ones.
